corrections.how: Which computer: (a) the Mac mini's own happy desktop, with the app running in happy's GUI session and attached to the existing npm gateway (attach-only; do not also start a CLI node on that Mac); (b) a clean macOS VM on the mini (MAC-03, the recommended target); (c) a parent's MacBook with the app in remote mode over the tailnet (MAC-12, not recommended). What to install: OpenClaw.app (needs macOS 15+) from the project's release downloads; the Homebrew npm gateway stays as it is. Enabling the bundled `cua-computer` plugin alone does nothing on macOS: its code throws unless the app supplies its private endpoint. Permissions go to OpenClaw.app, never to the shared `node` binary: Accessibility and Screen Recording, plus Event Posting for the default Peekaboo provider. The app's 'Allow Computer Control' switch starts ON. Gateway side: approve the device, then approve the node's command surface (`openclaw nodes pending` / `openclaw nodes approve`); `computer.act` is a macOS platform default, so no `gateway.nodes.commands.allow` entry is involved. Tool policy: the family runs `tools.profile: minimal` with sandbox mode all, so the one holder agent (MAC-02) needs `computer` in both `tools.alsoAllow` and `tools.sandbox.tools.alsoAllow`. Model: gpt-6-sol qualifies as the vision-capable model because OpenClaw only checks the model's catalog `input` list for image support, and the family's custom provider entries declare text and image; OpenAI's own model page lists image input too. Version: the v2026.9.7 release carries OpenClaw-2026.9.7.dmg, so the app can match the pinned gateway; the newest release (2026.10.1, published 10 Oct 2026) has no macOS app asset. Sandbox gate: `computer` is on the shipped sandbox default-deny list, and an explicit entry in `tools.sandbox.tools.allow` or `alsoAllow` removes it from that list. The per-person agents also deny `group:nodes`, which contains `computer` (the inbox agent denies every tool); the holder agent must not carry that deny.
caveats: Capture and input need a verified unlocked desktop. With FileVault on there is no automatic login, so after every reboot someone signs in by hand; a manual lock retires the running task and OpenClaw will not unlock the Mac.
macOS permission grants are tied to the app's signature, bundle id and path; the docs call them fragile and describe a stale Accessibility grant after app updates that needs remove and re-add.
Once the app is paired and granted, any agent that holds `computer` can drive that Mac with no per-action confirmation, because the app switch defaults on.

The three other desktop-control paths are not shortcuts: the `peekaboo` CLI skill needs the exec tool plus a bridge host; direct `cua-driver mcp` is a separately installed prerelease driver that OpenClaw neither installs nor polices; Codex Computer Use only serves Codex-mode agents, which this stack does not run.
Two similarly named tools are unrelated: `screen` only arranges Control UI panes, and `code_execution` is remote Python at xAI with no access to paired devices.
Some OpenClaw releases ship no macOS app asset (true of 2026.10.1), so the app version may trail the gateway. 2026.9.7 does ship one.

Pairing the app pairs a whole node, not one command. The same approval covers everything the app declares: shell execution on that Mac (`system.run`, governed by the app's exec approvals, which start at full access with no prompts on an unconfigured node), Desktop sharing (`desktop.stream`, on by default), screenshots and the widget panel. Set the app's exec approvals to deny and switch Desktop sharing off before approving the pairing.

corrections.how: Add `computer.act` to `gateway.nodes.commands.deny` in happy-config. A deny entry always wins over platform defaults and allow entries, withholds the command together with the node's `computer` capability, and is logged. Keep `computer` absent from every agent's tool lists; the per-person agents already deny `group:nodes`, which contains it, and the inbox agent denies every tool. For reference, the documented gate stack for screen control is: tool policy exposes `computer` to an agent; gateway command policy (deny list, and the allow list for the separately listed dangerous commands); device pairing and then a second, distinct approval of the node's command surface (a single-use setup link or SSH-verified pairing approves the first surface automatically; the family has SSH verification off and should not use setup links for a Mac); the switch inside the Mac app; and the macOS permissions. Exec approvals are not in that list: they gate shell commands on a node (MAC-10), not clicks. Off switches during a pilot: (1) put the deny line back (command-policy changes reach connected nodes under the default hybrid reload); (2) the G005 kill file checked in the desk hook; (3) on the Mac, turn off 'Allow Computer Control' (rechecked at each invocation) or revoke Accessibility. The widget-panel commands (`canvas.present`, `canvas.navigate`, `canvas.hide`) are allowed by default for a paired OpenClaw.app, and the documented agent path is `show_widget` with `presentation.target: "node_panel"`. But OpenClaw exposes `show_widget` only when the originating client declares the `inline-widgets` capability (the Control UI and the native apps) or a current-channel presenter matches (Discord Activities). Other channel runs do not receive the tool, and scheduled jobs get a pinned-only surface that cannot set `presentation.target`. An iMessage text or a 06:45 job therefore cannot open the panel. The plugin's separate `canvas` tool only presents, hides or navigates to an existing hosted document, and it is on the sandbox default-deny list.

corrections.how: An in-house tool plugin in the gateway process (same pattern as home_weather, which uses `definePluginEntry` and registers a tool; the SDK's `defineToolPlugin` helper is the tool-only alternative). Each tool spawns a fixed argument list, for example `osascript` with a bundled script file and one validated argument, or `shortcuts run` with a name from an allowlist and an input file path. Arguments are checked in code (enumerations, length caps, URL allowlist). No agent gets the general exec tool. The Automation consent for each target app is granted once by hand in happy's session. Held by the stateless home agent proposed for F076 to F078; output-only verbs could sit on a parent's agent.
caveats: Works only for apps that expose scripting commands or Shortcuts actions. Scripts that click through another app's interface need Accessibility for the calling process, which here would be the shared node binary; leave those out.
If the same commands were routed through the exec tool with an allowlist instead of a plugin, inline `osascript -e` forms should be made approval-only with `tools.exec.strictInlineEval`.
Verbs act on happy's account only. Shortcuts on the parents' own phones already run their personal automations better.
No verb may send, buy, unlock or open a door; those stay on the never list.
The plugin SDK entry helpers are marked experimental; pin and retest on each OpenClaw update.
If macOS attributes the Automation consent to the shared `node` binary (unverified), everything that binary runs inherits control of those apps, the same concern the docs raise for Accessibility.

corrections.how: The target Mac runs a node whose exec approvals are set to allowlist with no prompts and a deny fallback before pairing. The allowlist has one entry: the script's absolute path with an `argPattern` that fixes the permitted arguments. `openclaw approvals allowlist add --node ...` only adds a path pattern, so write the whole approvals document (allowlist security, no prompts, deny fallback, and the one entry) with `openclaw approvals set --node <id> --file <json5>`, and leave no path-only entry for the same script beside it, because unmatched arguments would fall back to that. On the gateway the holder agent's exec is pointed at that node explicitly (`tools.exec.host` node, `tools.exec.mode` allowlist, `tools.exec.node` bound). The holder is the stateless home agent, not a parent's memory-holding agent. The script is owned by an admin and not writable by the node's user.
caveats: On happy's own account there is almost nothing to tidy. The value requires pairing a parent's Mac, and a paired node extends gateway-operator power onto that Mac.
An unconfigured node starts with full execution and no prompts; the allowlist must be in place first.
macOS can make directory listings hang until Desktop, Documents and Downloads access is granted to the exact process doing the work.
A weekly launchd job running the same script needs no agent at all and is the simpler answer.
From sandboxed sessions exec does not route to a node on its own; the host must be set explicitly.

A CLI node started with defaults advertises more than exec: it shares that Mac's desktop when Screen Sharing is on (`desktop.host.enabled` defaults to enabled on CLI nodes) and publishes skills, plugin tools and MCP servers. Start it with an explicit `--commands` list limited to the exec commands.
The holder would be the first agent in this stack with the `exec` tool; no agent has it today.

That Mac needs token-based node auth to the gateway (Tailscale identity is not accepted for nodes). A single-use setup link avoids copying the shared token but approves the first command surface automatically, so the exec allowlist has to exist before the link is used.

corrections.how: The bundled File Transfer plugin on the gateway, with `plugins.entries.file-transfer.config` listing that node and `allowReadPaths` / `allowWritePaths` for the single folder and symlinks not followed. The MacBook's node is started with an explicit `--commands` list containing only the file commands; an explicit list also switches off computer use, skills, plugin tools and MCP on that node. Limit is 16 MiB per file. Fetched files are read by a tool-poor reader agent, not directly by the parent's memory-holding agent. The file commands (`file.fetch`, `dir.list`, `file.write`, plus `file.stat`, `dir.fetch` and `file.create`) are registered as dangerous plugin node commands, so the ones in use must also be added to `gateway.nodes.commands.allow`. The agent-facing tools are `file_fetch`, `dir_list`, `dir_fetch` and `file_write`.
caveats: Sending the file to Happy as an iMessage attachment (F001) already does this from any Apple device with one drag; build HappyDrop only if a real need survives that comparison, such as larger files.
The MacBook has to be awake and on the tailnet.
Fetched content is untrusted external content.
A denied path rejects a whole directory fetch rather than being filtered out.
The MacBook needs token-based node auth to the gateway; Tailscale identity is not accepted for nodes.
unverified: That a CLI-started macOS node whose `--commands` list holds only the file commands still advertises them. The bundled plugin registers them as node-host commands and is enabled by default, but this was not run.

caveats: A personal laptop has signed-in banking, mail, a password manager and the parent's Apple Account on screen or one click away.

On the default macOS provider, screen-coordinate scrolling is foreground input at the pointer, and CUA desktop input also uses the foreground route, so the agent and the person at the keyboard get in each other's way.
Both vendors tell developers to keep logins and sensitive data away from a computer-use model, and published red-team work shows such agents following instructions planted on screen.
If a parent insists on a one-off: attended only, switch 'Allow Computer Control' on for that sitting and off after, watch the whole run, and close every money or password window first.

corrections.safety: desk has no memory and the file returns only to the parent who asked. What the hook can enforce: the `url` of `browser_navigate` against a site allowlist, and a block or approval on `browser_type`, `browser_set_input_files` and `browser_download`. It cannot see the page, so it cannot tell a password field, a 2FA prompt or a CAPTCHA from any other input, and it does not see where a clicked link leads; those refusals rest on the agent's instructions and on a parent watching. reason: Confirmed as a not-recommended entry; all 7 sources check out. Presence is harmless but answers a question this household does not need an agent for, and Logbook is continuous screen capture sent to a cloud model.

source_checks.note: Anchor on the line: a recent-activity hint, not proof of which computer sent a message.
Anchor on the line (sentence spans 106-109): only idle duration and source are sent, no keys, coordinates, app names or window titles.
Anchor on the line; line 23 says enabling the plugin opts the gateway into capture.
Anchor on the line: default interval 30 seconds; up to 16 frames per 15-minute window go to the vision model.
Anchor on the line: sampled screenshots go to the configured vision route, which need not be local.
Anchor on the line: the bundled Codex plugin must be enabled and authenticated.
Fetched. Under 'App & Website Activity' a parent can see most-used apps and websites, set a Screen Time schedule and time allowances, through Family Sharing.

caveats: Presence is a recent-activity hint, not proof of who is at the keyboard, and only Macs running the app report it. It answers a question nobody in a four-person house needs an agent for.
For children, Apple's Screen Time through Family Sharing already gives app and website activity and limits, with nothing sent to an AI provider.

Logbook would send continuous pictures of a family member's screen to a cloud model. For a child's Mac that collides with the rule against cloud models for kids' content; for an adult's Mac it is surveillance of everything on screen, including banking and mail.
Logbook depends on the Codex plugin and its login, which this stack does not use.

Logbook does not need OpenClaw.app: once the plugin is on, a headless macOS node gets a `logbook.snapshot` command backed by the system screenshot tool. Keep the plugin disabled on any gateway that has a Mac node paired.
